blocks.prompt: How the Ball Got Its Shape
blocks.text: A rugby ball is shaped like an egg, not a circle. But it was not always made that way on purpose. The very first rugby balls were made from a pig's bladder, blown up with air. A pig's bladder is long and rounded, so the ball came out oval too. A man named Richard Lindon made these balls near Rugby School in England. Blowing up pig bladders was smelly and could make you sick, so Lindon made a rubber one instead. He also built a pump to fill it with air.

blocks.prompt: The Shape of an Accident
blocks.text: Every ball has a shape that suits its game. A soccer ball is round so it rolls true along the ground. A rugby ball is oval, and that shape started almost by accident. The first rugby balls were made from a pig's bladder that was blown up until it was firm. A pig's bladder is not round. It is long and lumpy, so the early balls were oval too. The game itself was named after Rugby School in a town called Rugby, in England. A local craftsman named Richard Lindon made balls for the school. Inflating a pig's bladder by mouth was unpleasant and could spread disease, so Lindon invented a rubber bladder and a brass pump to fill it. Over the years the oval shape turned out to be useful. A player can tuck the ball under one arm and run, throw a long spinning pass, and boot it high into the air. The pointed shape also makes the ball bounce in odd directions, which keeps every game unpredictable.

blocks.prompt: An Accident That Became an Advantage
blocks.text: Most balls are round, and for good reason. A round ball rolls in a straight line and bounces back the same way it fell, which is exactly what you want in games like soccer or basketball. The rugby ball breaks that rule. It is a stretched oval, closer to an egg than a globe, and its odd shape has a surprisingly ordinary origin. The first rugby balls were not designed at all. They were pig bladders, inflated with air until they were firm and then wrapped in leather. A pig's bladder is naturally long and uneven, so the balls came out plum shaped rather than round. The sport had grown up at Rugby School, in the English town of the same name, and a shoemaker named Richard Lindon supplied the school with balls. Inflating a raw bladder by mouth was foul work, and it may have made his wife seriously ill, so Lindon developed a rubber bladder and a pump to replace it. What began as an accident became an advantage. An oval ball can be tucked under one arm while a player sprints, spun into a long flat pass, or kicked in a tight spiral that cuts through the wind. When it hits the ground, it refuses to bounce predictably, skipping sideways and forcing players to react. A shape that started with a pig's insides now defines how the whole game is played.

blocks.prompt: The Ball a Pig Designed
blocks.text: Nearly every ball you can name is a sphere. A sphere rolls evenly, bounces back the way it came, and behaves the same no matter which way you turn it. Those are useful traits, so most sports settled on the round ball long ago. Rugby is the strange exception, and the reason lies in how its ball was first made. In the early 1800s there were no factories turning out matched, molded balls. A ball was a pig's bladder, blown up with breath until it was taut, then sewn into a leather casing to protect it. A pig's bladder is not a neat sphere. It is elongated and lopsided, so the finished ball ended up oval, somewhere between an egg and a plum. Nobody chose that shape. It was simply the shape of the material. The sport took its name from Rugby School, in the English Midlands town of Rugby, where an early version of the game was played. A local bootmaker, Richard Lindon, made balls for the pupils. Inflating diseased pig bladders by mouth was genuinely dangerous, and the work is often blamed for the illness that killed his wife. In response, Lindon developed an inflatable rubber bladder and a brass pump, which freed the ball from the pig entirely and let makers control its size and firmness. Once the shape could be chosen on purpose, players discovered it was better than round for their game. An oval tucks neatly against the body when you run, leaves the hand in a long spinning pass, and can be kicked in a spiral that flies far and straight. On the bounce it becomes wonderfully unreliable, kicking off at angles nobody can predict, which rewards quick reactions and keeps the play open. A ball born from a farmyard accident had become a piece of precise sporting equipment, and modern versions are molded from synthetic panels with a dimpled surface for grip, though the egg shape has never changed.

blocks.prompt: An Accident Preserved on Purpose
blocks.text: Almost every ball in sport is a sphere, and the reasons are practical. A sphere rolls in a straight line, rebounds along a predictable path, and presents the same face to a player no matter how it is turned. Soccer, basketball, tennis, and golf all took the round ball for granted. Rugby is the great exception. Its ball is a prolate spheroid, a stretched oval with two blunt points, and understanding why reveals how much of sport is shaped by accident rather than design. In the early nineteenth century, before molded rubber and modern factories, a ball was an inflated animal bladder inside a leather shell. The bladder of choice came from a pig. A pig's bladder is not round. It is long, curved, and uneven, and so the ball built around it came out oval, roughly the shape of a plum. No inventor sat down and decided a football should be egg shaped. The shape was inherited from the animal, and everything that followed grew out of that inheritance. The sport was named for Rugby School in the Warwickshire town of Rugby, where a distinctive handling game developed in the 1800s. The school bought its balls from a local bootmaker named Richard Lindon. Blowing up a raw bladder by mouth was revolting and hazardous, because a diseased bladder could carry infection, and Lindon's wife is often said to have died from the work. Whatever the exact cause, Lindon responded by inventing an India rubber bladder and a brass hand pump, replacing the pig's insides with a material a maker could trust and repeat. For the first time, the size and firmness of a ball could be chosen rather than simply accepted. Here the accident turned into a design. Once makers controlled the shape, they kept the oval, because players had learned to love it. An oval ball tucks cleanly under one arm at a sprint, spins off the fingers into a long flat pass, and can be struck in a tight spiral kick that holds its line through the air. When it lands it does something no round ball will do: it bounces unpredictably, darting sideways and rewarding whoever reacts fastest. A shape that began as a limitation had become the reason the game felt the way it did. Modern rugby balls have left the farmyard entirely. They are built from synthetic panels bonded and stitched together, dimpled all over so wet hands can hold them, and made in different sizes so that small children and grown adults each get a ball that fits. Yet for all that engineering, the silhouette has not changed. The ball a professional kicks today is still, in outline, the pig's bladder that a schoolboy once tucked under his arm, an accident preserved on purpose because the game grew up around it.
